title: Barossa Shiraz
subtitle: Australia's icon
objectives: Explain the role of old vines
Explain how Penfolds Grange changed Australian wine

steps.title: Ripe and rich
steps.body: The Barossa Valley, north-east of Adelaide, is warm and dry. Shiraz there is full-bodied, around 14.5 to 15% alcohol, with ripe blackberry, plum, chocolate, liquorice and often American oak's vanilla and coconut. Tannins are soft and ripe. It's the style that made Australian Shiraz famous worldwide.

steps.title: Old vines
steps.body: Phylloxera never reached South Australia, so the Barossa has some of the oldest Shiraz vines in the world, some planted in the 1840s by Silesian settlers. Old vines give low yields and concentrated fruit. The Barossa Old Vine Charter classifies Old Vines at 35 years and Ancestor vines at 125 years or more.

steps.prompt: Why does the Barossa have such old Shiraz vines?
steps.explanation: Strict quarantine kept phylloxera out, so the original ungrafted vines survive.

steps.title: Grange
steps.body: In 1951, Max Schubert, Penfolds' chief winemaker, made an experimental Shiraz after visiting Bordeaux. Penfolds Grange, aged in new American oak, was first mocked, then celebrated. It became Australia's most famous wine and showed that Shiraz could make world-class, long-lived wines.

steps.explanation: Barossa Shiraz is deeply coloured and full, not pale.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Barossa Shiraz is ripe, full and chocolatey
Old ungrafted vines date back to the 1840s
Penfolds Grange, from 1951, made Australian Shiraz world-class
